questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Structural Chromosomal Abnormalities' refers to.
questions.a: A chromosome can break and heal in four tell-tale ways: deletion trims a segment away as in retinoblastoma on chromosome 13, duplication repeats a stretch as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease on chromosome 17, inversion flips a piece through 180 degrees leaving the length unchanged as in RCAD syndrome, and translocation moves a piece onto another chromosome - mutually as in Burkitt lymphoma between chromosomes 8 and 14, or one-way in the Robertsonian type that lowers the chromosome count.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Structural Chromosomal Abnormalities'.
questions.a: Shorter, longer, flipped or relocated - the breakage pattern names the aberration and points to the disease.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Structural Chromosomal Abnormalities' taught, and from which source text?

Explain in your own words what 'Numerical Abnormalities and Polyploid Sets' refers to.
questions.a: Whole chromosomes can be lost or gained: monosomy removes one of a pair, trisomy adds one, both counts of aneuploidy - as against polyploidy, where entire sets multiply so a human-count genome would hold 69 in triploid or 92 in tetraploid form; crop breeding exploits this, giving hexaploid bread wheat, tetraploid cabbages and mustards, triploid banana and apple, and octoploid strawberry and sugarcane.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Numerical Abnormalities and Polyploid Sets'.
questions.a: Add one for a trisomy, subtract one for a monosomy, and multiply the haploid number by set count for polyploids.

Explain in your own words what 'Down Klinefelter and Turner Syndromes' refers to.
questions.a: Three karyotypes anchor human cytogenetics: trisomy 21 gives Down syndrome with flat face, palmar crease and low IQ and one extra chromosome in 47,XX+21 or 47,XY+21; an extra X in 47,XXY males yields Klinefelter syndrome with tall stature, small testes and a single Barr body on buccal smear; and monosomy X in 45,X females gives Turner syndrome with short stature, webbed neck and no Barr body.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Down Klinefelter and Turner Syndromes'.
questions.a: Count the sex chromatin: one Barr body betrays the extra X of Klinefelter, none marks the missing X of Turner.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Down Klinefelter and Turner Syndromes' taught, and from which source text?

Take the relation taught for 'Incidence Rates of Chromosomal Syndromes' and work with: births = 12, down_rate = 15, klinefelter_rate = 25, male_births = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of klinefelter_cases.
Explain in your own words what 'Incidence Rates of Chromosomal Syndromes' refers to.
questions.a: Each syndrome carries a headline frequency - about one Down baby per 800 live births, one Klinefelter male per 1000 newborn boys, and one Turner girl per 2500 newborn girls - so dividing a birth cohort by the rate predicts how many affected newborns a hospital or district should expect.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Incidence Rates of Chromosomal Syndromes'.
questions.a: Divide the birth total by each syndrome's rate denominator to forecast case counts.

Explain in your own words what 'Monogenic Disorders and Pedigree Mapping' refers to.
questions.a: Over ten thousand human illnesses trace back to a single faulty gene and therefore follow Mendelian rules, sorted by whether the mutant allele sits on an autosome or the X and by dominance - autosomal recessive sickle cell anaemia and cystic fibrosis, autosomal dominant achondroplasia and Huntington disease, X-linked recessive haemophilia and Duchenne dystrophy, X-linked dominant hypophosphatemia; a family tree drawn with standard pedigree symbols reveals which rule applies.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Monogenic Disorders and Pedigree Mapping'.
questions.a: One gene, four inheritance routes - autosomal or X-linked, dominant or recessive - and the pedigree tells you which.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Monogenic Disorders and Pedigree Mapping' taught, and from which source text?

Explain in your own words what 'Carrier Crosses in Recessive Disease' refers to.
questions.a: Two healthy carriers of a recessive allele - each S/s at the sickle locus, say - gamete three genotype classes in their children: one quarter affected s/s, half carriers S/s, and one quarter clear S/S, so risk counselling for such couples starts from the quarter-and-half split.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Carrier Crosses in Recessive Disease'.
questions.a: Quarter affected, half carriers, quarter clear - the fixed forecast of a carrier-by-carrier mating.

Take the relation taught for 'X-linked Transmission Probabilities' and work with: children_total = 400. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of affected_sons.
Explain in your own words what 'X-linked Transmission Probabilities' refers to.
questions.a: Sex chromosomes give the transmission its asymmetry: a carrier mother passes a recessive X to half her sons, an affected father hands his X to every daughter but no son, and in the dominant form an affected mother likewise shares the trait with half of both her sons and daughters.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'X-linked Transmission Probabilities'.
questions.a: Halve the children for sons, then halve again for those inheriting the affected X.

Explain in your own words what 'Polygenic Disorders and Mitochondrial Inheritance' refers to.
questions.a: Several genes acting together produce the common chronic disorders - diabetes mellitus where type 2 makes up about ninety percent of cases against ten percent for insulin-dependent type 1, hypertension staged from 120 over 80 upward, and coronary heart disease built by atherosclerotic plaques; separately, mutated mitochondrial genes ride the egg alone, so severity tracks the mix of faulty and healthy mitochondria and only mothers transmit the disease.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Polygenic Disorders and Mitochondrial Inheritance'.
questions.a: Nine of every ten diabetics are type 2; and a mitochondrial father transmits nothing - only the maternal line matters.
